commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-five sources, including two CHAI frameworks rated as must, endorse a limited-scale pilot with phased go-live and heightened monitoring before full deployment of higher-risk AI, but no supplied study tests whether this practice reduces system-wide harm. The recommendation rests on expert consensus and analogy to general implementation practice rather than on comparative evidence.

perspectives.view: No supplied study compares piloted with unpiloted rollouts, and no study documents the hazard itself. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The endorsements agree in direction, but agreement among commentaries and frameworks does not substitute for measured outcomes.

Several endorsing commentaries describe pilots as a way to surface integration problems and adapt tools to local workflows before scale-up. None reports pilot duration, monitoring burden, or fidelity data, so the supplied sources give teams no empirical basis for sizing a pilot or setting go-live thresholds.

The CHAI frameworks list prospective evaluation on live production data and incident monitoring as must-level controls. One commentary on FDA oversight proposes a phased introduction period in which algorithms operate alongside clinicians. These statements reflect proposed or voluntary standards, not binding regulatory requirements identified in the supplied material.

One endorsing roadmap for inclusive chatbots calls for small-scale implementation before wider use. No supplied study reports how pilots perform for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients, so the evidence cannot show whether pilot sites represent these groups.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare phased, monitored pilots against direct full-scale deployment of higher-risk AI and measure harm events, time to detection, and rollback frequency. Such studies should also report pilot size, duration, monitoring intensity, and staffing cost so that health systems can judge what a sufficient pilot requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems that pilot at well-resourced sites may miss failure modes that appear only when a tool reaches these patients, and pilot site selection may need to account for this.
